title: The rich man's library
hookLine: Calvisius Sabinus bought slaves to memorize Homer for him (Letters 27)
carry: nobody can learn it for me

lines: A RICH MAN WITH A POOR MEMORY.
cards: There's a man in Seneca's Rome named Calvisius Sabinus. He's very rich, he wants badly to seem cultured, and his memory is so poor that he sometimes forgets the names of well-known heroes he's trying to mention.
So he comes up with a plan only money could buy: he'll purchase education the way he purchases furniture. In the twenty-seventh letter, Seneca tells the story with a straight face.
It's also, a little, about saving an article to read later and never reading it.

teach.b: Sabinus buys enslaved men and has each one learn a poet by heart: one knows Homer, another Hesiod, and nine more, one for each of the Greek lyric poets.
Seneca says they cost a fortune, because none were to be had, so they had to be made to order.

Sabinus keeps them at his feet while he entertains, asking them for lines to quote, and still gets the lines wrong halfway through. He has decided, Seneca says, that whatever anyone in his house knows, he knows.
A guest named Satellius Quadratus teases him: you should take up wrestling. Sabinus protests that he can barely stay alive, he's so frail. Don't say that, comes the reply.
Look how many healthy slaves you have. The point lands. You can't outsource strength, and you can't outsource understanding.
And plainly: these were people, owned and made to perform. Seneca tells it as a joke about Sabinus; slavery itself gets a straight look in a few days.

teach.h: A SOUND MIND CAN'T BE BOUGHT.
teach.b: Seneca's line: a sound mind can't be borrowed or bought. In Latin, bona mens nec commodatur nec emitur.

teach.h: NOBODY CAN LEARN IT FOR ME.
teach.b: And if it were for sale, he adds, there would be no buyers, while bad sense is bought every day. A shelf of books, a playlist of lectures, a friend who knows: all good.
But somebody has to do the learning, and it can only be you.

how: Some people who study the Stoics memorize a few short lines, so the ideas are at hand when they're needed rather than stored on a shelf.

o: a Roman poet who knew all of Homer by heart
a rich Roman who tried to buy a memory
Seneca's friend who taught him wrestling

games.q: you're Sabinus's dinner guest. he says he's too frail for wrestling. what's the joke Seneca reports?
o: look how many healthy slaves you have.
games.why: Satellius Quadratus's jab exposes the plan: strength and understanding can't be owned through someone else.

practice: Pick one short thing you've been meaning to know rather than just have: a line from a poem, a verse, the name of the tree outside. Say it slowly once, then again with your eyes closed, then once more.
Notice the moment it moves from the page into you.

wordCard.voice: Calvisius Sabinus. The rich Roman who bought slaves to memorize poetry for him, proving Seneca's point: a sound mind can't be bought. Today's word.
